transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, I'm Dr Okonjo, one of the emergency doctors. Can you confirm your name and date of birth for me?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Harriet Fenwick-Doyle, fourteenth of March, ninety-one.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thanks, Harriet. What's happened today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've done my ankle in. I went over on it coming down the stairs at work.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Ouch. When was that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About... it'd be about four hours ago? No, sorry, less than that. It was just after my ten o'clock meeting, so two hours, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, so around two hours ago. Which ankle is it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This one, the left.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And how did it happen exactly? Did your foot roll inwards?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah, it turned in under me. I missed the last step.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did you hit your head or black out at all?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, nothing like that. I just sort of sat down hard.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And could you walk on it afterwards?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not really, I hopped to the car. My colleague drove me in.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you managed any steps since you got here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I tried in the waiting room. I got maybe two steps and had to sit down.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any numbness or tingling in the foot?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, it just throbs.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you ever injured this ankle before?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any medical problems I should know about?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, I'm pretty healthy.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you take any regular medicines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just the pill. Microgynon.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. Any allergies to medicines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Penicillin. I come out in a rash.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any stomach ulcers, asthma or kidney problems?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, none of those.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What do you do for work?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm an office manager, so mostly desk based, but I do walk between two sites.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you smoke or drink?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't smoke. A few glasses of wine at the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Right, let me have a look. I can see some swelling over the outside of the ankle. I'm going to press on a few places. I'm pressing on the bony bit at the back of your left ankle, on the outside. Is that tender?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ow, yes, right there.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And the bone on the inside, here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What about this bone on the outside edge of your foot, the base of the fifth metatarsal?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, not there.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And the top of the foot here, the navicular?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Can you wiggle your toes for me? Good. Your foot's warm and I can feel the pulse on top of the foot. Can you feel me touching here, and here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I can feel that.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay. So, using what we call the Ottawa ankle rules: you're tender at the back of the outer ankle bone and you couldn't take four steps, which means we need an X-ray to check for a fracture.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do you think it's broken?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: It's possible. It may well be a bad sprain, but the X-ray will tell us. I'll request X-rays of the ankle, the AP and mortise views. For pain, I'm going to give you paracetamol, one gram, which you can take four times a day, no more than four grams in twenty-four hours. And ibuprofen four hundred milligrams three times a day with food, as you've no asthma or stomach problems.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Can I have something now? It's really sore.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Yes, the nurse will bring the first doses now. We'll pop a cold pack on it and keep it raised.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Whatever the X-ray shows, you'll go home with crutches, and I want you to keep it elevated as much as you can. If it's a sprain, we'll give you an advice leaflet and you can start gently moving it as the pain allows.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if it's broken?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Then it depends on the type of fracture. Many of these are managed in a boot, with an appointment at the fracture clinic. Let's see the pictures first.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: One important thing. If your foot goes cold, pale or numb, or the pain gets much worse and isn't controlled with the painkillers, come straight back.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Cold, pale or numb. Got it.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Also, because you're on the pill and you'll be less mobile for a while, if you get pain or swelling in your calf, or any chest pain or breathlessness, seek help urgently.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, I didn't know that. Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any questions for now?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, thank you.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Inversion injury to the left ankle descending stairs at work, approximately 2 hours ago.
reference_note.history: Missed the last step and foot rolled inwards. No head injury or loss of consciousness. Unable to weight-bear immediately after injury (hopped to car); managed only two steps in the department. No numbness or tingling. No previous injury to this ankle. No significant past medical history. Office manager, mostly desk-based, walks between two sites. Non-smoker; drinks a few glasses of wine at weekends.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Combined oral contraceptive (Microgynon). Allergic to penicillin (rash). No history of peptic ulcer disease, asthma or renal disease.
reference_note.examination: Swelling over the lateral aspect of the ankle. Bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the left lateral malleolus. Medial malleolus non-tender. Base of fifth metatarsal and navicular non-tender. Foot warm, dorsalis pedis pulse palpable, sensation intact.
reference_note.impression: Ottawa ankle rules positive (posterior lateral malleolar tenderness; unable to weight-bear four steps). Possible lateral malleolar fracture; differential diagnosis ankle sprain.
reference_note.plan: X-ray left ankle (AP and mortise views). Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g four times daily (maximum 4 g in 24 hours) and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food; first doses given in the department. Cold pack and elevation. Crutches. If sprain: discharge with advice leaflet and early mobilisation as pain allows. If fracture: management according to fracture type, likely boot and fracture clinic referral.
reference_note.safety_netting: Return immediately if the foot becomes cold, pale or numb, or if pain is not controlled with analgesia. Advised of increased VTE risk with reduced mobility while taking the combined pill: seek urgent help for calf pain or swelling, chest pain or breathlessness.

mutations.seeded_rationale: A wrong-side record can lead to the wrong ankle being imaged or reviewed at follow-up, and the patient may not notice.
mutations.description: Examination recorded on the wrong ankle

mutations.description: Penicillin allergy dropped from an ED note

mutations.seeded_rationale: The patient corrected four hours to two; the timing has little bearing on ankle management, so harm is unlikely.
mutations.description: Injury time kept at the figure the patient corrected

mutations.seeded_rationale: Recorded paraesthesia suggests neurovascular compromise that was not present, which may trigger unnecessary investigation or obscure a later genuine change.
